synopsis: ICMM (International Council on Mining and Metals) is identified as a user of the nine-level control model; its joint April 2024 Leading Sites work with EMESRT treats intervention as one layer of controls, not a silver bullet [f11737, f390, f6550]. Effective Level 8–9 implementation requires understanding the Level 1–7 baseline during normal operations and integrating intervention technology with existing site controls rather than replacing them [f702, f2589, f11750, f704]. ICMM and EMESRT call for scenario-based functional-performance requirements, while mining requirements often exceed legal minima through demands for heterogeneous-fleet and third-party interoperability [f703, f2580]. ICMM's ICSV goal was to make collision avoidance technology available to mining companies by 2025 using EMESRT requirements, but the facts do not establish whether that goal was achieved [f2588]. The corpus flags implementation risks: human performance can improve or deteriorate after technology introduction, and unqualified Level 9 deployment can harm production and accelerate brake wear, against the backdrop of South African clauses brought into force in December 2022 despite readiness concerns [f581, f2892]. Research coverage remains uneven: no ICMM study applying the named road-derived scenario/testing frameworks to off-road machines was found, Chapter 12 did not review ICSV, and Chapter 13 treated ICMM as an unverified lead [f1698, f9809, f11206].

relations.note: Both require understanding Level 1–7 effectiveness before implementing Level 8–9 controls.
Both establish the lower-level baseline as prerequisite to higher-level controls.
Both prioritize Level 1–7 baseline before Level 8–9 implementation.
Both reject technology or intervention as a silver bullet.
Integration with existing controls reinforces that higher levels cannot replace lower levels.
Layered controls provide the rationale for integrating intervention with existing site controls.
Adds implementation sequencing and nonreplacement principles to the nine-level model.
Variable human responses explain why technology alone cannot guarantee safety.
Production losses and brake wear illustrate limitations of technology-only deployment.
Risks of unqualified deployment reinforce establishing baseline controls first.
Adds heterogeneous-fleet and third-party interoperability to the integration requirement.
Chapter 3 reports an ICSV goal; Chapter 12 explicitly did not review that programme.
A specific ICMM programme claim contrasts with Chapter 13's unverified-lead status.
